# Andaz — Market Simulation and Customer Reality Check

**Date:** 3 November 2026
**Method:** synthetic 1,000-person panel, 50 illustrative voices, 5 fictional expert critics, a qualitative verdict and three field experiments.
**Reproducibility:** every count in Step 4 is computed from `panel.csv`, which is generated by `build_panel.py` (seed `20261103`). Change an assumption in the script and every table changes with it.

> This is a synthetic simulation. The personas are fictional. Nothing below is evidence of real demand, and no real person was interviewed.

---

## 0. Executive summary (read this if nothing else)

- **The concept is strong for a narrow group and weak for everyone else.** In the conservative baseline, 27.5% of the full panel would use Andaz at least once, but only 6.1% would return weekly or more, and 3.6% say they would pay. Among the 562 panellists who fall inside the target audience, "would use" rises to 39.7% and "would pay" to 6.0%. Simulated, not measured.
- **The two problems people care about most are not the ones the product currently leads with.** Panellists keep asking "where does this price come from, and is it an asking price or a real deal?" and "why must I register before I see anything useful?" The repository already separates asking prices from verified prices with discipline, but the advisor, portfolio and valuation all sit behind a verified-phone account, and the three free guest questions described in the brief do not exist in the code I could inspect.
- **The "AI advisor" in the repository is a structured intake interview, not an open question-answer assistant.** In Sorani it uses no language model at all. If the live site matches the repository, the AI positioning promises more than the product delivers and the panel's AI-sceptics punish that gap.
- **Consumers will mostly not pay; professionals and the diaspora might.** Stated willingness among payers clusters around 0.5–1.0 USD per question for consumers, 5–15 USD for a one-off valuation report, and 20–40 USD per month for investors and agents. None of this is a revenue forecast; it is what fictional people claim they would do.
- **Verdict: 5 / 10.** The engineering discipline around data honesty is unusual and valuable. The commercial model, the registration wall, and the thin data supply are the risks that could sink it. Recommendation: resolve the data-supply and guest-value uncertainty before investing further, and narrow the first audience.

### 1.3 Information supplied only by the brief (not verified)

- The names "Andaz" and "Mulk Wallet", the tagline "The True Value of Property", and the two domains.
- The three-free-questions guest offer, the credit/billing system, and paid AI usage.
- That the platform is "under active development", and the specific list of target users.

### 1.4 Assumptions used in the simulation

- The live Andaz site exposes, at minimum, the homepage, project profiles, the map and the market page to guests, and gates the advisor and portfolio behind registration, consistent with the repository's architecture.
- The AI advisor behaves as in the repository (structured interview, evidence-grounded recommendations, lead capture), with free-form questions available to a limited degree.
- Pricing of paid services is unknown; panellists react to the *idea* of paying, and state amounts unprompted.
- Exchange rate for conversions in quotes: roughly 1,310 IQD per USD (my assumption for readability, not a market fact).

### 1.5 Claims I could not verify

- Anything about the live site's design, speed, content volume, number of published projects, or whether any verified transaction prices have ever been published.
- Whether AI responses are accurate or useful in practice.
- Whether any payment has ever been collected.
- Whether the repository I inspected is the code actually serving andaz.krd.

### 1.6 Local context used for panel design (with sources)

- **Population.** The October 2024 federal census counted about 2.52 million people in Erbil governorate and about 6.5 million in the Kurdistan Region; Erbil and Baghdad have historically published different figures ([Peregraf](https://peregraf.com/en/news/10297), [Shafaq](https://shafaq.com/en/Kurdistan/Kurdistan-Region-s-population-exceeds-14-of-Iraq-s-total), [PUKmedia](https://pukmedia.com/EN/Details/75514)).
- **Connectivity.** Internet penetration in Iraq was 81.7% at the start of 2025 (38.0 million users) and 83.8% in the Digital 2026 report ([DataReportal 2025](https://datareportal.com/reports/digital-2025-iraq), [DataReportal 2026](https://datareportal.com/reports/digital-2026-iraq)). Facebook is used by roughly 70% of the population, skewing male and 25–34 ([NapoleonCat](https://napoleoncat.com/stats/facebook-users-in-iraq/2025/12)). Smartphone share by OS is **assumed** Android-heavy; no source found.
- **Household finances.** Roughly 70% of Kurdistan Region households are reported to depend on government salaries, which were repeatedly delayed through 2025 ([Shafaq](https://shafaq.com/en/Report/Decade-long-standoff-salary-crisis-sparks-public-outcry-in-Iraqi-Kurdistan), [Peregraf](https://peregraf.com/en/report/9165), [LSE](https://eprints.lse.ac.uk/130368)). This drives the panel's income distribution and its price sensitivity.
- **Payments.** Digital payments are growing but Iraq remains cash-heavy; trust, fees and interoperability are cited obstacles ([Iraq Business News](https://www.iraq-businessnews.com/2025/06/02/modernising-iraqs-financial-infrastructure-the-rise-of-digital-payments/), [Jummar](https://jummar.media/en/8136), [AGBI](https://www.agbi.com/banking-finance/2026/06/zaincash-ceo-iraq-is-5-years-behind-in-digital-payments/)). The panel's 44% "has a wallet or card" is an assumption consistent with that picture.
- **Housing supply.** The Board of Investment reported more than 52,000 units under construction in Erbil in April 2025, 367 housing projects underway, and a pause on new housing licences since February 2024 ([Kurdistan24](https://www.kurdistan24.net/en/story/862888/367-housing-projects-underway-as-erbil-moves-to-24-hour-electricity), [invest.gov.krd](https://invest.gov.krd/news-and-events/kurdistan-region-s-construction-boom-what-investors-need-to-know/)). The Rudaw Research Center counted 131 residential projects and about 128,500 units over two decades ([Rudaw RC](https://rudawrc.net/en/pdf/article/erbils-real-estate-boom-over-50000-new-apartments-houses-and-vilas-under-construction-2024-03-24)). The US State Department notes the Board has moved away from approving real estate licences because of oversaturation ([State Dept 2025](https://www.state.gov/reports/2025-investment-climate-statements/iraq)).
- **Prices.** 2025 reporting describes sharp land-price rises linked to the Green Belt and water projects, based on broker anecdotes ([Kurdistan24](https://www.kurdistan24.net/en/story/856204/green-belt-and-water-project-spark-real-estate-boom-in-erbil), [Erbil Business News](https://erbilbusinessnews.com/erbil-real-estate-prices-water-greenbelt/)). Crowd-sourced Numbeo data (119 entries) puts central Erbil at about 1.5 million IQD per m² ([Numbeo](https://www.numbeo.com/property-investment/in/Erbil-Irbil-Iraq)). No official transaction-price series was found, which is itself a finding: the gap Andaz targets is real, and so is the difficulty of filling it.
- **Alternatives.** Homele claims 30,000+ listings, 700,000 downloads and 1,800 agents, though figures conflict across sources ([iraqtech.io](https://iraqtech.io/homele-iraqs-ai-enabled-platform-for-your-real-estate-needs/)); OpenSooq Iraq, Baghy Shaqlawa, Paya, Dar Erbil, Sypo, Maskani, Eqarat Iraq and Naxsha also operate ([OpenSooq](https://iq.opensooq.com/en/erbil/property/villas-palaces-for-sale), [Baghy Shaqlawa](https://baghyshaqlawa.net/en), [Paya](https://paya-realestate.com/en/search/properties/for-sale/Erbil)). Facebook groups, Telegram channels and personal brokers as the dominant channel is an **assumption**; I found no measurement.
- **Legal.** Property sales are registered with the KRG Ministry of Justice (registration fee listed at 2% of estimated value) and official valuation references Law No. 85 of 1978 as amended ([services.gov.krd](https://services.gov.krd/en/service/moj-08-en)). I found **no** published KRG broker-licensing regime and no data-protection statute specific to this use; both need local legal verification. A private guide's "about 5% broker commission" is unofficial.

## STEP 1 — The 1,000-person panel

### 1.1 How the panel was built

The panel is generated, not sampled. Each of the 1,000 rows draws its attributes from the distributions below; the reaction model in `build_panel.py` then scores each person from those attributes plus seeded noise. This guarantees internal consistency (someone who "would pay" always also "would or might use"; someone who "would not use" never returns) but it is **not statistically representative** of Erbil. There is no defensible sampling frame for this population, so treat every percentage as "share of this fictional panel".

**Evidence-informed distributions:** age skew toward 18–44 (young population), Android-dominant devices, 56% cash-only, low-to-middle household income with a public-sector-heavy occupation mix, Sorani as the majority language with Arabic and Badini minorities. **Pure modelling assumptions:** digital skill, reading confidence, numeracy, decision style, AI attitude, housing tenure, buying readiness, and the share of agents, developers and investors (deliberately over-weighted relative to the real population so that professional segments are large enough to read).

---

## STEP 2 — Realism rules applied

1. **Imposed stress-test constraint.** Thresholds in the reaction model were set so that at least 40% of first reactions are indifferent, confused or negative. The baseline landed at **59.9%** non-positive (negative 24.9%, indifferent 20.1%, confused 14.9%). This is a design choice, not a discovered statistic. Section 4.9 shows what changes when the constraint is removed.
2. **Forced realism overrides.** 45% of low-digital-skill panellists are classified "confused" regardless of score (they would not get past the map or the registration flow). 35% of agents are classified "negative" regardless of score (price transparency threatens their margin). Everyone else follows the score.
3. **Liking is not using, using is not paying.** Payment intent is only possible for people who would or might use; return frequency is only possible for people who would or might use; "once" is the modal return pattern for consumers.
4. **Multiple objections allowed.** The mean panellist raises 3.6 objections. Percentages in Step 4.3 therefore exceed 100% in total.
5. **Misunderstandings are built in.** 20.6% expect a listings site with phone numbers; 14.0% find the name uninformative; some owners expect an official valuation.
6. **Cash, time, trust and family.** 56% cannot or will not pay online; 32.6% default to a broker, relative or Facebook group; 44.6% have no current need and are judged accordingly.
7. **Agents and consumers are modelled with opposing incentives.** Agents are the only segment with a "threat to my business" objection, and the minority of agents who do adopt are modelled as heavy, weekly users.

---

## STEP 3 — Fifty detailed voices

**How these were chosen.** Fifty rows were drawn from `panel.csv` by segment, with a deliberate spread of first reactions inside each segment. Strong supporters and harsh critics are therefore **over-represented** relative to the panel (the panel is 21% positive and 25% negative; this selection is closer to 30% / 30%). Names, jobs and personal details are invented to fit each row's attributes. Amounts quoted are what the fictional person *says*; conversions use roughly 1,310 IQD per USD.

Format per voice: **ID · name** — profile · personality · first reaction · likes · worries · use? · pay? · prediction · what changes their mind.

---

### Active buyers (0–6 months)

**P0158 · Rebaz, 23, male.** Junior clerk in a government office in Erbil, lives with his parents, who are about to buy a flat with him as co-owner. Household income 500–1,000 USD. Skeptical by nature, dislikes AI, high digital skill but low reading confidence and little property vocabulary. iPhone, has a FIB wallet.
- *First reaction:* "Another website that tells me what a flat costs? My cousin's broker already tells us what it costs, and he can actually get us the keys."
- *Likes:* the map with project boundaries; the asking/verified separation once it was explained to him.
- *Worries:* "who checked these prices?", being asked to verify his phone before the advisor says anything, too much text on each screen, and the idea of paying for an answer at all.
- *Use?* **Maybe**, once, to double-check a price his father's broker quotes.
- *Pay?* **No.** "Information about my own city should not cost money."
- *Prediction:* "It will fail because people here buy through people, not through screens."
- *Changes his mind:* a verified sale price for the exact building he is looking at, visible without logging in.

**P0002 · Shler, 58, female.** Secondary-school teacher, owns her house in Erbil, buying a small apartment for her son's marriage within months. Low digital skill, low reading confidence in long text, but good with numbers. Skeptical; indifferent to AI. Android, ZainCash.
- *First reaction:* "I opened it and saw a map and some English-looking numbers. Where are the apartments for sale? Where do I call?"
- *Likes:* "if the prices are really in one place, that saves me a week of phone calls."
- *Worries:* source of prices, registering before seeing anything, very few projects listed, prefers her brother-in-law's advice, finds the screens crowded, expected a listings site.
- *Use?* **Maybe**, during this purchase only, if her son drives.
- *Pay?* **No.**
- *Prediction:* "It will fail unless they make it as simple as the Facebook groups."
- *Changes her mind:* a single large button that says "apartment prices in Erbil" in Sorani and lands on a plain list.

**P0475 · Nasreen, 59, female.** Senior public employee in Shaqlawa from a well-off family, looking to buy in Erbil for retirement within six months. Low digital skill, impatient, resistant to AI, pays in cash.
- *First reaction:* "I tried for two minutes and left. I don't know what Andaz is and I don't have patience for a chatbot."
- *Likes:* the "stalled / delayed" warnings on projects, which she heard about from her nephew.
- *Worries:* registration, stale data, no agent to call, distrust of AI, complexity.
- *Use?* **No.** She will ask her nephew to look.
- *Pay?* **No.**
- *Prediction:* "It will fail with people my age and maybe succeed with the young ones."
- *Changes her mind:* nothing on a phone. A printed report from someone she trusts, possibly.

**P0503 · Hiwa, 47, male.** Part-time master's student and former shop owner in Sulaymaniyah, living with family, planning to buy in Erbil for his daughter's university years. Skeptical, cautious about AI, cash only.
- *First reaction:* "Interesting. I want to see whether the prices match what the brokers in Erbil are telling me by phone."
- *Likes:* prices in one place; proper Sorani.
- *Worries:* no way to contact the seller; it is information, not a transaction.
- *Use?* **Maybe**, while deciding.
- *Pay?* **Maybe.** Would pay about 800 IQD per question (≈0.6 USD) or about 15,000 IQD (≈12 USD) once for a written comparison of three projects, paid through a relative's wallet.
- *Prediction:* "It will succeed only if Erbil brokers start quoting it. Otherwise nobody in Sulaymaniyah will know it exists."
- *Changes his mind:* seeing the same price quoted by the site and by two brokers.

**P0064 · Ahmed Jasim, 50, male.** Arabic-speaking public employee transferred to Erbil, lives in employer housing with four children, buying his first home in Erbil within months. Practical, cautious, high digital skill, Android, cash only.
- *First reaction:* "Finally something in Arabic that shows the projects on a map with prices. I don't know anyone here, so this is exactly what I need."
- *Likes:* everything about the project profiles; construction status; the map.
- *Worries:* registration, whether the data is current, "what does Andaz mean?", no way to pay online, expected to be able to call the developer from the page.
- *Use?* **Yes**, several times a week until he buys.
- *Pay?* **Yes.** About 2 USD per advisor question, about 3 USD for a valuation summary, about 2 USD per month if there were a subscription, but only if he can pay cash at a shop or via a relative's card.
- *Prediction:* "It will succeed with people like me who have no family network in Erbil."
- *Changes his mind:* a listed phone number for each project's sales office.

**P0820 · Dilshad, 30, male.** Private-sector employee who returned from the UK, owns a modest house in Erbil, needs something bigger within six months. Low digital skill despite living abroad, practical, resistant to AI, prefers English, cash only.
- *First reaction:* "Looks fine. I'll still use my mate who's an estate agent."
- *Likes:* the idea of tracking his own house's value.
- *Worries:* paying for information; no online payment habit; habit of asking people.
- *Use?* **No.**
- *Pay?* **No.**
- *Prediction:* "Won't matter either way. People here won't pay for a website."
- *Changes his mind:* if his agent friend used it in front of him.

### Future buyers (6–24 months)

**P0109 · Mohammed, 32, male.** Badini-speaking manager in a public institution, high income, owns an apartment in Erbil and has owned before, plans to move to a villa in two years. Low digital skill, practical, cautious.
- *First reaction:* "The Kurdish is not my Kurdish and the map asked me to allow my location. I closed it."
- *Likes:* portfolio tracking; comparing areas, in principle.
- *Worries:* source of prices, registration, thin data, no listings.
- *Use?* **No**, at least not now.
- *Pay?* **No.**
- *Prediction:* "It will fail in Duhok and might work in Erbil."
- *Changes his mind:* Badini interface, and an explanation of what the location permission is for before it is asked.

## STEP 4 — Summary of the full 1,000-person panel

Every number in this step is a **simulated outcome under the stated assumptions** (conservative baseline, seed 20261103). Denominators are stated in each table.

### 4.1 Adoption and payment

**First reaction (denominator: 1,000).**

| Reaction | n | % |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Positive | 213 | 21.3 |
| Curious | 188 | 18.8 |
| Indifferent | 201 | 20.1 |
| Confused | 149 | 14.9 |
| Negative | 249 | 24.9 |
| **Non-positive total (imposed ≥40%)** | **599** | **59.9** |

**Usage and payment intent (denominator: 1,000).**

| | Would pay | Might pay | Would not pay | **Total** |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| **Would use** | 30 | 98 | 147 | **275 (27.5%)** |
| **Might use** | 6 | 57 | 197 | **260 (26.0%)** |
| **Would not use** | 0 | 0 | 465 | **465 (46.5%)** |
| **Total** | **36 (3.6%)** | **155 (15.5%)** | **809 (80.9%)** | **1,000** |

**Trying once versus returning (denominator: 1,000).**

| Return pattern | n | % |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Never (would not use) | 465 | 46.5 |
| Once | 238 | 23.8 |
| Occasionally, around a property decision | 236 | 23.6 |
| Regularly (weekly or more) | 61 | 6.1 |

Of the 61 regular returners, 24 are investors, agents or developers, 25 are active or future buyers, and 12 come from the remaining groups (casual browsers, owners, diaspora, rest of Iraq, no current need). Consumers return around a decision, then leave. That is the shape of the demand: **episodic for consumers, habitual only for professionals.**

**Target audience versus everyone else.**

| | Core target (n = 562) | Outside target (n = 438) |

**Reading the table.**
- **Consumer demand** is concentrated in 211 people (active plus future buyers): 60% would use, but only 7.6% would pay. They want the product free at the moment of decision.
- **Professional demand** is small and split. Investors are the most enthusiastic and the most willing to pay for a recurring service. Agents are polarised: most reject it as a threat, but the minority who embrace it are heavy users and the likeliest monthly payers. Developers would pay for *control of their own data and leads*, not for information.
- **Owners curious about value** are a weaker segment than the brief assumes. Without a sale in view they have no reason to return, and they expect an official-grade valuation that an estimate range cannot give.
- **Diaspora** are the best consumer payers per capita and the strongest "I will research this myself" motivation, but they cannot pay with Iraqi methods and will not pay before seeing a track record.
- **Strongest plausible initial customer segment:** Erbil active and future buyers (211 people) as the *users* who create value, and individual investors plus data-contributing agents (83 people) as the *payers*. Trying to monetise the consumers directly is the weakest path in this simulation.

### 4.5 Hidden risks

1. **Data supply is a human pipeline.** Every public price passes through CSV import, human review and publication. The marginal cost of freshness scales with the number of projects. If the operator cannot sustain weekly updates, objection 8 becomes objection 1. The 52,000 units under construction and 367 projects in Erbil are far more than one small team can keep current by hand.
2. **Verified transaction prices may be legally or practically unobtainable.** The registry (Ministry of Justice) holds "estimated value" figures for fee purposes, which may differ from real consideration; access rules for bulk data are unknown. Without them, "verified" shrinks to "self-reported by a developer or broker", which the panel will eventually notice. **Requires local legal verification.**
3. **Valuation language.** Law No. 85 of 1978 governs official real estate valuation; whether a private platform may publish something called a "valuation" without a licensed appraiser, and what disclaimers are required, is **unverified**. The repository's own wording ("an estimate, not an appraisal") is prudent; the brief's tagline "The True Value of Property" is not.
4. **AI advice and liability.** A user who buys on the strength of an advisor answer and loses money will blame the platform. The code's refusal to let the model produce numbers is the right instinct; the marketing should match it.
5. **Personal data.** Portfolios hold encrypted addresses, prices, documents and sometimes exact coordinates; the advisor transcript records what a household can afford. Iraq and the Kurdistan Region lack, to my knowledge, a comprehensive data-protection statute; the absence of law is not the absence of risk, especially if Telegram or WhatsApp verification data is involved. **Verify.**
6. **Commercial conflict.** An advertising module and a marketplace module exist in the codebase. The moment a sponsored project appears beside an "independent" price, trust collapses for the analytical minority that is also the paying minority (P0579, P0182).
7. **Competition from distribution, not from features.** Homele and the brokerage apps have agents and listings; Facebook groups have habit. Andaz's edge is honesty, which is hard to demonstrate in an advertisement.
8. **Name collision.** "Andaz" is also a Hyatt hotel brand; two panellists assumed a hotel. In Sorani, *endaze* (ئەندازە) means "measure" or "estimate", which is apt, but Arabic speakers get no meaning from it. **Trademark exposure in Iraq: verify.**
9. **Economic timing.** With roughly 70% of households on repeatedly delayed public salaries, consumer willingness to pay for information is likely to be at a low point; licence issuance for new housing projects has been paused since early 2024, which may slow the flow of *new* projects to profile.
10. **Hosting and performance.** Shared hosting, cron-driven queues and a 2,900-line map page are a plausible source of slow first loads on mid-range Android phones over mobile data. Unverified, but the panel's "too complex" objection would be amplified by slowness.

### 4.6 Common misunderstandings and how to prevent them

| Misunderstanding | Why it happens | Clearer communication |
| --- | --- | --- |
| "It's a listings site; where do I call?" | Every alternative is a listings site; the map looks like one. | A first-screen sentence: "Andaz does not sell property. It shows you what projects really cost so you can negotiate." Link to developer contact where known. |
| "It's a brokerage or a developer's advert." | No visible "who we are and how we make money". | A short, permanent "independence" statement; label paid placement loudly if it ever exists. |
| "The valuation is official." | The word "valuation" means a stamped document here. | Call it "estimated value range"; show sample size and confidence first; state what it can and cannot be used for. |
| "The AI knows the market." | "AI advisor" promises a knowledgeable agent. | Describe what it is: "guided search over published data; it never invents a price". Show the evidence card before the answer. |
| "The price shown is what I will pay." | Asking and verified are labelled, but small. | Put the label *inside* the price chip ("Asking · 85,000 USD"), never beside it. |
| "Andaz is a hotel / a wallet / a bank." | Name and former name. | Sorani and Arabic tagline under the logo on every screen. |
| "It covers Kurdistan." | The brand says `.krd`. | Say "Erbil, for now" on the homepage and the map's empty states. |

### 4.7 Price sensitivity (simulated statements, not purchase evidence)

Denominators: people in the segment who said they would or might pay. "Zero" is the share of the whole segment that would pay nothing. Amounts are what people *say*; only a purchase test (Step 6) can confirm them.

| Segment | n (segment) | Would / might pay (n) | Zero payment | Per advisor question (USD, p25 / p50 / p75) | One-off valuation or comparison report (USD) | Monthly professional account (USD) |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- | --- | --- |
| Active and future buyers | 211 | 68 | 67.8% | 0.34 / 0.60 / 0.90 | 3 / 6 / 11 | 0 / 1 / 3 |
| Diaspora | 52 | 15 | 71.2% | 0.90 / 1.35 / 2.52 | 4 / 13 / 18 | 0 / 2 / 3 |
| Individual investors | 40 | 19 | 52.5% | 0.50 / 0.60 / 0.90 | 4 / 5 / 7 | 9 / 22 / 38 |
| Agents / brokers | 43 | 8 | 81.4% | 0.38 / 0.50 / 0.90 | 7 / 15 / 15 | 18 / 22 / 30 |
| Developers / professionals | 32 | 5 | 84.4% | 0.30 / 0.45 / 1.05 | 9 / 12 / 20 | 12 / 30 / 100 |
| Owners curious about value | 67 | 8 | 88.1% | 0.30 / 0.45 / 0.90 | 2 / 3 / 4 | 0 / 0 / 2 |
| Casual, no need, rest of Iraq | 555 | 68 | 87.7% | 0.30 / 0.45 / 0.90 | 2 / 6 / 12 | 0 / 1 / 3 |

**Interpretation.**
- Consumers anchor a question at roughly **500–1,200 IQD** and a report at **5,000–15,000 IQD**. These are "newspaper" prices, not "lawyer" prices. A per-question credit priced above about 1 USD will be rejected by most of the panel's consumers.
- The only plausible recurring revenue is professional: **20–40 USD per month** for investors and agents, **30–100 USD** for developers, and only if the service brings them *leads or control*, not just information.
- 56% of the panel is cash-only. Any price list is irrelevant to them until cash top-ups through agents, shops or a relative's wallet exist.
- The three-free-questions offer is **directionally right** (objection 4 is about getting nothing before registering) but the panel's natural free threshold is "see prices without an account", not "ask a bot three times".
- **Not a revenue forecast.** Multiplying these figures by panel shares would produce a number with no empirical basis.

### 4.9 Sensitivity to assumptions

**What changes when the conservative constraint is removed.** The same model without the forced "confused" and "agent negative" overrides and with thresholds relaxed by 0.5 gives: non-positive first reactions 46.9% (from 59.9%); would use 29.1% (from 27.5%); might use 35.6% (from 26.0%); would not use 35.3% (from 46.5%); would pay 4.4% (from 3.6%); might pay 19.1% (from 15.5%); weekly return 6.9% (from 6.1%). Active buyers' "would use" rises from 69% to 83%; investors' "would pay" from 17.5% to 20%; agents barely move.

**Conclusions that hold in both scenarios (more robust):**
- Usage is episodic for consumers and habitual only for professionals.
- Paying is rare in the full panel (under 5%) and concentrated among investors, active buyers and diaspora.
- The top five objections are identical in both runs: price source, broker/family habit, no need, registration wall, paying for information.
- Agents are polarised regardless of thresholds.

**Conclusions that depend heavily on assumptions (validate first):**
- The *size* of the willing-to-pay group (3.6% vs 4.4%) depends on the income distribution and the cash-only share, both assumed.
- The "confused" share depends on the assumed 21% low-digital-skill population and on how the live interface actually behaves, which I could not see.
- Agent willingness to pay depends on an assumed partnership model (leads, branded reports) that does not yet exist in the code.
- Diaspora payment depends entirely on an international card path, which is unverified.
- Everything about data freshness depends on how many verified prices actually exist on the live site today: zero, dozens, or hundreds produce different products.

## STEP 5 — Five expert critics (fictional, outside the panel)

**E1 · Farhad Qadir, property investor, 25 years in Erbil and Sulaymaniyah.** "The problem is real: I have never once seen a transaction price in this city that I did not have to extract from someone's cousin. But asking prices are noise, and verified prices will not come from developers, who have every reason to hide discounts. If Andaz cannot get registry data or a critical mass of brokers submitting closed deals, its 'verified' index will stay thin forever and I will keep using my phone book. I would pay 50 dollars a month tomorrow for a weekly sheet of real closings by area. I would pay nothing for a chatbot."

**E2 · Soran Rashid, founder of a competing Iraqi listings platform (fictional).** "They have built the honest version of what we all pretend to be, and I respect that. But honesty is not a distribution channel. We have thousands of agents uploading because uploading gets them calls; Andaz gives agents nothing, so agents give it nothing, and a price database without a supply engine decays in six months. The AI advisor is a mistake in positioning: in this market a consumer's trust is in a face and a phone number, and 'AI' reads as 'nobody is accountable'. If I were them I would white-label the price intelligence to brokerages and let the brokerages be the face."

**E3 · Dr. Lana Ahmed, marketing and consumer behaviour specialist, Erbil.** "The brief describes nine target groups; a launch can carry one. The simulation and common sense agree: the person who changes behaviour is the buyer in the next six months who is afraid of overpaying, and the person who pays is the investor or the agent. The registration wall before any value is the single largest leak, and 'three free questions' misreads the barrier: people do not want to ask a bot, they want to see a number. The name needs a Sorani and Arabic tagline on every screen, because 'Andaz' means 'estimate' only to Kurds who think about it, and means a hotel to everyone who searches for it. Finally, formal Sorani signals government, not help; the copy should sound like a knowledgeable friend."

**E4 · Hiwa Mustafa, lawyer specialising in property and commercial matters in the Kurdistan Region (fictional; nothing here is legal advice).** "Three things need verification before scale. First, the word 'valuation' and the tagline 'The True Value of Property': official valuation is a regulated act under Law 85 of 1978 as amended, and a court or a buyer may treat a published figure as a representation; the product's own 'estimate, not an appraisal' wording is safer than its marketing. Second, personal data: there is no comprehensive data-protection law to comply with, which means the platform's own consent records and encryption are its only defence when a dispute arises over a leaked portfolio or an advisor transcript. Third, paid advice: if the advisor's output can be read as investment advice and a user pays for it, consumer-protection and liability exposure increase, and the disclaimers must be in Sorani and Arabic, not only in English. None of this is a reason to stop; all of it is a reason to put a local lawyer on retainer before the first paid credit is sold."

**E5 · Rebin Karim, long-time user of property apps and Facebook groups, bought three times in Erbil.** "I have used every app, and I still buy through a person. What apps gave me was a feeling that I had done my homework, and that feeling is worth something, but not a monthly fee. Andaz would have saved me from one bad project if the delay warning had existed in 2019, so that feature alone is worth a lot. The rest of the panel is right that I will not pay per question; I will pay once, maybe 15,000 dinars, for a one-page report I can show my father. And if the app ever shows a 'sponsored' project, I will assume all its prices are bought."

**Where the experts disagree, and what evidence settles it.**
- *Is AI an asset or a liability?* E2 and E3 say liability in positioning; E1 and E5 are indifferent; E4 sees legal exposure. Settle with an A/B landing test: "know the real price" versus "AI advisor" (Experiment 1).
- *Who pays?* E1 says investors for data; E2 says brokerages for white-label; E5 says consumers for a one-off report. Settle with Experiments 2 and 3.
- *Can verified prices be obtained at all?* E1 and E2 doubt it. Settle by attempting to collect 50 closed-deal prices from 10 brokers in 30 days, and by a legal inquiry into registry data access.

## STEP 6 — Final verdict

### 6.1 Score: 5 / 10 (qualitative assessment, not a probability)

**Why not lower:** the product attacks a real information failure that the panel, the experts and the public record all confirm; the engineering around price provenance, confidence and project status is more honest than any alternative I know of in this market; Sorani-first is a genuine differentiator; the diaspora and active-buyer segments show clear pull.

**Why not higher:** the data pipeline is manual and thin until proven otherwise; every high-value feature sits behind a verified-phone registration wall; the AI positioning overpromises relative to the code; consumers will not pay and professionals are not yet given a reason to; the name requires explanation; the economic moment is hostile to paid information; and I could not observe the live product at all.

### 6.2 Single biggest plausible cause of failure

**Thin, stale, or unverifiable prices.** If a buyer checks three projects they know and finds one missing, one out of date, and one labelled "asking" with no verified figure, the product's entire claim ("the true value") is falsified in their first session, and they return to the broker. Everything else is secondary to this.

### 6.3 Single biggest plausible driver of success

**Becoming the place Erbil buyers check before they call a broker, because it shows an honestly labelled price and the project's real status, in Sorani, without an account.** Once a meaningful share of buyers arrive at brokerages with Andaz screenshots, agents and developers are forced to engage, and engagement is the supply engine that solves 6.2.

### 6.4 Five practical changes, ranked by likely impact

| # | Change | User problem it addresses | How to check it worked |
| ---: | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | **Guest-first value.** Show project prices, price type labels, area intelligence and project status to anonymous visitors on the first screen. Keep the account only for saving, portfolio and lead submission. If a free-question allowance is kept, make it visible and actually guest-accessible (the inspected code has no guest path). | Objection 4 (registration wall) and 1 (price source invisible before login). | Share of new mobile visitors who view at least two project prices in their first session ≥ 50%; registration conversion measured *after* value is seen, not before. |
| 2 | **Build the supply engine before building more features.** Recruit 20–30 brokerage offices and 5–10 developers as named data partners; give them a free professional account in exchange for weekly price submissions; show "updated N days ago" on every price (the `age_days` field exists); hide prices older than 90 days behind a "may be stale" state. | Objection 8 (thin or stale data), and E1/E2's core criticism. | Share of published projects with a price updated in the last 30 days ≥ 70%; number of verified (closed-deal) prices per month, target 50 in month three. |
| 3 | **Reposition the advisor as guided search, and make price labels unmissable.** Rename "AI advisor" to something like "Find what fits my budget"; show the evidence card before the recommendation; put "Asking" or "Verified" inside the price chip; write the Sorani copy in conversational register and have a native reviewer approve it. | Objections 6 (AI distrust), 1 (price source), 9 (expectation gap), and the Sorani-register complaint. | Interview completion rate ≥ 60%; click-through from recommendation to project profile ≥ 40%; in moderated tests, 8 of 10 participants can say, unprompted, whether a shown price is asking or verified. |
| 4 | **Three taps to a price on a 360-pixel phone.** Make "Know the price where you are" or a plain Sorani search box the hero; defer the map's layers, compare mode and heat map behind a "More" control; measure and cap first-load weight on mobile data. | Objection 7 (complexity), and the unverified performance risk. | Median time from landing to first price seen under 20 seconds on a mid-range Android over 4G; Largest Contentful Paint under 3 seconds on a throttled connection. |
| 5 | **Monetise professionals and one-off reports, not consumer questions.** Professional accounts for agents, investors and developers (leads, branded comparison reports, data correction rights, area reports); a one-off, cash-payable valuation or comparison report for consumers; keep basic questions free. Add cash and local-wallet payment paths before any price list is published. | Objections 5 (paying for information) and the cash-only majority; aligns incentives so agents feed data. | Ten paying professional accounts within 60 days of launch; one-off report purchase conversion ≥ 5% of users who request a valuation. |

### 6.5 Three inexpensive real-world experiments

**Experiment 1 — Positioning and first-screen value (landing test).**
- *Hypothesis:* Erbil buyers respond more to "see the real price" than to "AI advisor", and will browse prices without an account.
- *Recruit:* 25–44-year-olds in Erbil governorate via Sorani and Arabic social ads (Facebook, Instagram, Telegram channels), budget about 300–500 USD over two weeks.
- *Show:* two landing variants, A "Know the real price of any Erbil project" and B "Ask the AI property advisor", each leading to a guest-accessible page with five real project prices labelled asking or verified.
- *Measure:* click-through rate, share of visitors viewing two or more prices, share tapping "see all projects", and share that registers when asked *after* viewing.
- *Threshold:* a variant with CTR ≥ 2.5% and ≥ 30% of visitors viewing two or more prices is a pass; a difference of more than ten percentage points between A and B decides the positioning.
- *Next action:* if A wins, rename and re-lead the homepage; if B wins, invest in advisor quality; if neither passes, the proposition itself needs revision before any further building.

**Experiment 2 — Concierge paid report (purchase test).**
- *Hypothesis:* owners and buyers will pay a one-off fee for a plain-language valuation or three-project comparison report, at "newspaper" prices.
- *Recruit:* 60 people who ask a price question in Erbil Facebook groups or through partner brokers, plus 20 diaspora contacts.
- *Show:* an offer over WhatsApp: a one-page Sorani or Arabic report produced manually from Andaz data within 24 hours, priced at 10,000 IQD for half the group and 25,000 IQD for the other half, payable by FIB, ZainCash, Qi or cash to a partner office; diaspora offered 10 USD by card.
- *Measure:* actual payments, not stated interest; repeat requests within 60 days; whether the report is forwarded to others.
- *Threshold:* ≥ 20% pay at 10,000 IQD, ≥ 8% at 25,000 IQD, ≥ 15% of diaspora pay by card.
- *Next action:* pass → productise the report as the consumer paid tier; fail → drop consumer monetisation and treat consumers as the free audience that feeds professional demand.

**Experiment 3 — Agent and developer supply pilot.**
- *Hypothesis:* small and mid-size agents will submit prices weekly in exchange for a professional account, and a third will pay for it afterwards.
- *Recruit:* 15 brokerage offices and 5 developer sales offices in Erbil, approached in person.
- *Show:* a free 60-day professional account with a simple weekly price-submission form (asking and, where available, closed prices), a branded comparison report, and visibility of leads that mention their office. At day 60, offer the account at 25,000–40,000 IQD per month.
- *Measure:* weeks with at least one submission per office; number of verified prices submitted; conversions to paid at day 60; whether submitted prices differ systematically from public asking prices.
- *Threshold:* ≥ 10 of 20 offices submit in at least 6 of 8 weeks; ≥ 5 of 20 convert to paid; ≥ 50 closed-deal prices collected.
- *Next action:* pass → the supply engine exists, scale to 100 offices and build the professional dashboard properly; fail → verified prices are not obtainable from agents and the "true value" claim must be replaced by a more modest asking-price-plus-status proposition, or registry access must be pursued legally.

### 6.6 Direct recommendation

**Resolve a critical uncertainty before investing further, and narrow the target audience.** Do not add features. Spend the next 60–90 days proving two things: that verified or at least weekly-fresh prices can be collected for a meaningful share of Erbil projects (Experiment 3), and that anonymous buyers will come, browse prices and return when the first screen gives them a labelled number without an account (Experiment 1). Treat Erbil active and future buyers plus the diaspora as the audience to delight for free, and investors, agents and developers as the customers to charge. Keep the asking/verified discipline and the project-status honesty exactly as they are; they are the moat. Revise the AI framing and the registration wall; they are the leak.

---

*This is a synthetic simulation designed to uncover blind spots and generate testable hypotheses. It is not a real survey, verified customer feedback, or evidence of actual market demand.*
